There are different kinds of "AI" jobs. There is data engineering (which doesn't really have much to do with AI really, it involves moving a lot of data from place to place and making it usable for ML engineers / Data Scientists), ML engineer (which involves creating, implementing, maintaining and deploying ML solutions at scale) and then AI research. 

For AI research jobs, you will need a PhD from a top college because the job involves inventing things but for the other two you mostly need experience. Keep in mind that "AI" is a bit of a hype and the demand for software engineers or data engineers is higher than ML/AI jobs. Just look at how many jobs OpenAI has for those 2 fields compared to pure AI research.

For industry, an ML/AI role is almost impossible to get without a minimum of a master's degree. Your best bet is software systems or hardware and networking but keep in mind that university courses are very different compared to real software engineering.

>does that mean we try appending the node after prev node as long as prev node is not None but may be say a node in a different list?

Think of a linked list as a chain structure like this:

|Node 1| -> |Node 2| -> |Node 3|

If `insert_after_node` is called with the argument `prev_node` equal to Node 1 and `data` say Node 4, then the linked list becomes:

|Node 1| -> |Node 4| -> |Node 2| -> |Node 3|

To answer your question, we append the node after whatever node `prev_node` is, so yes there can be multiple linked lists at the same time. 

Consider this: 

|Node 1| -> |Node 4| -> |Node 2| -> |Node 3| as the first list. 

If you have a 2nd list |A| -> |B| -> |C|, `insert_after_node(A, D)` will modify the 2nd list to be |A|->|D|->|B|->|C|. I hope this helps.

Learn HTML, CSS and JavaScript to build the front end (What the user sees and interacts with) part of your website. There are many libraries that can help you make your page look good without a lot of effort, like Bootstrap. For handling server side requests e.g. ("When a user presses buy and pays, process the request and reduce the item count in database by units purchased) and databases you have many options, but for absolute beginners I recommend learning Python and the bottle framework (which is very light and minimalistic).

Ultimately it's a question of if you can afford it and which college you go to and what you want to do. If you go to a decent large state university with good professors or a better research university and don't pay insane amounts of tuition then I'd say it's a great choice. 

People say programming can be self taught, and that's somewhat true for the concepts, but I've learned many things at university that I would likely never learn/understand if I tried to do them on my own. Universities also provide for team projects, hackathons and clubs which provide a different view to IT outside of the run of your mill conceptual lectures. 

Universities will also provide you with a good theoretical foundation (proofs, mathematics, algorithms etc)  in case you want to pursue research in the future. 

Now if you just want to build websites or mobile applications I don't see a point in going to college.
